text: I sort the stack of printed invoices by due date, clipping the ones that match and sliding the rest into the green tray. The printer behind me hums through a page every few seconds, and I let it finish without checking. Pencil marks run down the margin where I've ticked each line.

Our team lead wheels her chair over to my desk and sets down a single sticky note with a room number on it. I nod, finish the sentence I'm typing, and save the file under today's date. Outside the window a delivery van idles, then pulls away, and the light on the carpet shifts a little toward the door.

The spreadsheet has four hundred rows and I work down them one at a time, matching each code to its column without skipping ahead. When a cell has a stray space I trim it, and when the next row matches I move straight on. At half past three the radiator clicks on under the window, and I hardly look up.

I stand at the whiteboard and copy the week's dates into a grid, one marker color for each team. The cap of the blue marker has gone missing, so I use the green and keep going. Someone down the hall laughs at something, and I hear the chairs roll back and forth on the tile.

I slice the onions into thin half-moons on a damp cutting board, letting the knife find its own rhythm. The pan on the back burner has already warmed, and the oil ripples when I tip it. I scrape the pieces in with the flat of the blade and stir them slowly until they turn translucent.

Bread goes into the toaster and I wait with my elbows on the counter, watching the steam fog the window above the sink. When the lever pops up I butter the slice edge to edge, then cut it corner to corner. I eat the first half standing up, looking at the garden through the glass.

Dinner is a pot of lentils that has simmered since noon, and I lift the lid to check it every so often. Steam rises and smells of cumin and bay. I set two bowls on the table, tear a warm flatbread in half, and sit down across from my brother, who is already reaching for the salt.

At the market stall I lift a peach, press near the stem, and set it in the paper bag with the others. The vendor counts out my change into my palm one coin at a time. I eat a plum on the walk home, and its juice runs down my wrist while the sun warms the back of my neck.

The train is half empty at this hour, so I take the window seat and set my bag on the empty one beside me. Fields slide past in long bands of brown and green, and a line of poplars marks a river I can't quite see. Every few minutes the conductor's announcement rolls through the carriage, and I follow the names of the stations.

I drive the old road to work with the radio low and both hands loose on the wheel. The lights along the avenue turn green one after another, so I let the car roll at a steady speed. A cyclist passes on my left, and I leave him a full car length before I move back over.

Mid-morning the bus crosses the bridge and the water below flashes silver between the cables. I stand near the back door with one hand on the pole, swaying a little as we take the bend. A woman beside me is knitting a grey scarf, and her needles click in time with the wheels on the joins.

On the bike path the wind comes from behind me, so the pedaling feels light and my shoulders drop without my asking them to. I pass the bakery, the dog walker, and the row of plane trees dropping their seed fluff. At the lights I unclip, plant one foot, and wait with my helmet still on.

I kneel at the edge of the pond and dip the jar until it fills, then lift it toward the light. Tiny water beetles turn circles beneath the surface while a damselfly rests on a reed beside my knee. The reeds lean slightly with each breath of wind, and I keep my hands still for a long while.

The path up the ridge is dry and pale, and every few steps a grasshopper clicks away from my boots. Below me the valley opens in patches of ochre and dark pine. I stop at the cairn, drink from my bottle, and watch a hawk turn slow loops over the far slope.

Rain has stopped and the forest floor smells of wet bark and moss. I step carefully over a fallen log, my boots sinking slightly into the soft ground. Drops gather on every fern frond and fall one by one onto the leaf litter, and somewhere high above a thrush starts its song again.

At dawn the field is grey with frost, and my breath hangs in front of me as I walk the fence line. I count the sheep by their shapes in the mist, then check the gate latch with my glove. A kestrel drops over the hedge, and the first sun touches the top of the barn roof.

I fold the warm towels into thirds and stack them on the shelf in the hall, the largest on the bottom. The washer finishes its spin cycle and I move the damp sheets into the basket one armful at a time. Sunlight lies across the floorboards, and I follow it with the broom.

Dishes drip in the rack while I wipe the counter in long strokes from left to right. The sponge smells of lemon soap, and the tap runs warm over my wrists. When the sink is empty I dry the last pan, hang the towel on its hook, and switch off the kitchen light.

The vacuum drones along the hallway runner and I push it slowly, overlapping each pass by a hand's width. Dust lifts in pale strands where the light from the stairwell falls. I empty the canister into the bin, tap it twice on the rim, and clip it back in place.

I scrub the bathroom tiles one row at a time, starting at the top corner so the suds run down and rinse as they go. The mirror clears under my cloth, and the old grout lines grow whiter with each pass. I rinse the brush, hang it over the tub, and open the window to let the air in.

The nurse wraps the cuff around my upper arm and presses the button, and the band tightens with a soft rush of air. I watch the needle sink back toward zero on the dial while she writes a number on her clipboard. She says it looks fine, and I nod at the poster of the human heart on the wall.

The physio has me lift my leg slowly from the table, hold it for a count of five, then lower it again. Her hands rest lightly on my ankle to guide the motion. The window beside us shows a row of sycamores, and each time I lower the leg I notice how little effort the movement takes.

In the waiting room I sit by the fish tank and count the bubbles rising from the little plastic castle. My name is called on schedule, and I stand without hurry, gathering my coat and the folder of scans. The hallway smells faintly of disinfectant, and the doors swing shut behind me slowly.

The pharmacist counts the tablets into a small white bottle and slides it across the counter with the printed label facing up. I read the dose twice, tuck the bag under my arm, and step out into the afternoon. A bus sighs at the curb, and a gull rides the wind above the car park.

Once lunch is over, my sister folds the tablecloth and passes me one corner so we can shake out the crumbs together. Her son is building a tower from the dessert spoons, and the grown-ups let him keep going. Someone opens the back door, and the warm air carries in the smell of cut grass.

My old friend Ruth calls from the coast, and we talk for an hour about nothing much, the price of tomatoes and her neighbor's new fence. I stand at the kitchen window while we talk, watching a blackbird work through the lawn. When she laughs at my bad joke, the sound comes down the line clear as if she were in the room.

Down at the park, the dog keeps fetching a tennis ball my father throws, and the two of them return to the same patch of grass. I sit on the bench with my coffee, the paper cup warm against my palm. A neighbor waves from across the path, and I wave back without getting up.

At the bedside my grandmother tells the story of the lost ring again, and I let her reach the end without correcting the details. Her hand finds mine on the blanket and stays there. Through the open curtain I can see the nurses changing shifts in the corridor, and the afternoon light moves slowly up the wall.

I copy the diagram from the textbook onto graph paper, labeling each arrow with a neat little letter. The pencil lead scratches softly, and an eraser crumb rolls down the page. At the front of the room the teacher is writing on the board, and I follow her chalk marks one line at a time.

The library reading room is nearly empty, and the old radiator ticks as it warms. I turn the pages of the chemistry text slowly, running a finger under each equation. My notebook fills with small careful numbers, and when I reach the end of the chapter I check every sum twice.

The exam hall is still except for pens moving across paper and the clock above the door. I work through the first question, then the second, and make a small tick beside each one I've finished. At the far end a chair scrapes, and I keep my eyes on the next problem.

The seminar room has a window that looks onto the bike shed, and a student near me is drawing little boxes in the margin of her notes. I read the paragraph aloud when it's my turn, pausing where the commas fall. Afterwards I underline the line that made the professor nod, and I go back to the start.

I swim lengths in the early pool, my arms rolling over one after another in a steady loop. The water is cool and hushed against my ears, and the lane rope bobs gently beside me. At the wall I push off, glide, and feel my breath come back in long, even pulls.

The trail climbs through the birch wood at an easy grade, and my running shoes find the packed dirt without any fuss. Each stride lands in the same rhythm, and my ponytail swings in time. At the junction I take the left fork, the one with the small wooden bridge, and I keep going.

I roll out the yoga mat by the window and sink into the first pose, letting my weight settle through my heels. Sunlight warms the wooden floor, and a single bird calls from the feeder outside. I breathe in for four counts and out for six, following the instructor's voice on my phone.

On the rowing machine the handle thuds back and forth, and the flywheel hums a steady note under my feet. Sweat beads along my hairline, and I count the strokes off on the small screen. Near the end of the set I ease the pace down, and the monitor's numbers settle one by one.

I sand the arm of the old chair in slow circles, following the grain toward the joint. Fine dust drifts onto my sleeves and settles on the sawhorse. When the wood feels smooth under my palm, I wipe it with a damp cloth and set it by the workshop door to dry.

The leaking tap yields to a single turn of the spanner, and the drip stops mid-fall. I lift out the old washer, press the new one into its seat, and thread the nut back down by hand. Water runs clear through the spout when I open it again, and I hear it splash into the empty sink.

I thread the blue wool through the loom in orderly, tight rows, checking each knot against the pattern card pinned above me. The shuttle slides back and forth with a soft knock. By mid-afternoon the band of color has grown a hand's width, and the lamp throws its light across the weave.

I solder the last joint on the little circuit board, touching the iron to the pad for exactly two seconds. The solder flows bright and silver and settles into a neat cone. I trim the leads with snips, brush away the flux, and hold the board up to the lamp to inspect each joint.

The greengrocer lays a bunch of radishes on the scale and I watch the needle settle. I pick out two lemons, sniff the top of each, and tuck them into my cloth bag beside the bread. The sun is warm on the awning, and the stall owner hums a song I half recognize.

At the hardware counter I hand over the list, and the clerk disappears into the back aisles for a few minutes. I wait by the bin of loose screws, sorting them by size with one finger. He returns with the right washers in a paper envelope, and I check the count before I pay.

The post office queue moves one person at a time, and I shuffle forward with my parcel tucked under my arm. A child in front of me counts the stamps in the display case out loud. When my turn comes I slide the box across the counter, and the clerk weighs it without a word.

I push the cart down the supermarket aisle past the cereal boxes, reading each shelf label as I go. The wheel has a slight wobble that makes a soft tick on every rotation. At the end of the row I turn left toward the dairy case, and the cold air brushes my hands.

The ferry pulls out from the harbor slowly, its engine a low vibration through the deck rail. Gulls turn over the wake and the town shrinks behind us, white houses stacked on the hillside. I lean on the rail with my ticket still in my hand and watch the lighthouse slide past.

The hostel courtyard is strung with lanterns, and the owner brings me a glass of mint tea without being asked. I sit on the low stone wall with my notebook open, writing down the names of the streets I walked today. A moped buzzes past the gate, and somewhere inside a radio plays a slow old waltz.

Up here the road climbs in long switchbacks, and the coach tilts gently with each bend. I have no plans until dinner, so I simply watch the snowline creep down the slopes. A man across the aisle is peeling an orange in careful segments, and the scent drifts over to me.

With the boarding call still ten minutes away, I find a seat by the window and open my paperback. Planes taxi slowly past the glass, their lights blinking in the grey morning. I read one page, then another, and when the speaker crackles I don't look up until my row is called.

I tune the old guitar one string at a time, turning each peg until the note rings true against the reference tone. The wooden body hums faintly under my palm. Then I play the opening chords slowly, letting every note ring out before I move my fingers to the next shape.

On the watercolor sheet I drag a wide wash of blue across the top third, leaving the paper's grain to show through in places. Wet paint pools slightly at the bottom edge, and I tilt the board to let it drift. Water drips from my brush into the jar, and the studio radio plays a long piano piece.

I sit on the piano bench with my sheet music propped up and start the scale from the bottom. My left hand keeps a steady pulse while my right hand climbs, one note at a time, to the top of the keyboard. When the last note fades, I turn the page and go on.

The knitting circle meets in the back room of the community hall, and we pass a skein of green yarn from hand to hand. Someone is teaching a new member to cast on, slowly counting each loop aloud. My needles click in their own rhythm while the rain taps the high windows.

I scroll through the photo album on my phone, pausing on the picture of the harbor at dawn. I tap to share it with my mother, and the little progress bar fills in one smooth sweep. The screen dims a little, and I set the phone face down on the arm of the sofa.

The laptop fan whirs softly as I drag files into the new folder, one batch at a time. A progress window reports each copy in plain green text. When the last file lands, I eject the drive, close the lid, and listen to the fan spin down.

My phone buzzes once on the kitchen counter, and I glance at the preview before wiping my hands on the towel. It's the bakery confirming Saturday's order, with the loaf count and pickup time. I type a quick thumbs-up, then drop the phone back beside the fruit bowl.

On my tablet the draft saves itself as I type the last paragraph, and the cloud icon turns to a tick without any fuss. I close the cover and let the screen go dark. Outside the window a sprinkler clicks through its cycle, and the wet lawn gleams.
